title: Constant-factor randomized direct sums for total Boolean functions
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Is there an absolute constant \(c>0\) such that, for every pair of nonempty finite input sets \(X,Y\), every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\) and every integer \(k\ge1\), \[R_{1/3}(f^{\otimes k})\ge c\,k\,R_{1/3}(f),\] where communication is public-coin, worst-case and measured with one global error probability?

why: Direct sums ask whether communicating about many tasks together can save a substantial fraction of the single-task cost. They connect communication lower bounds with interactive compression and the distinction between information revealed and bits transmitted. The exact error and task conventions determine which savings are possible.

sentences: Alice and Bob must jointly compute a total Boolean function of their private inputs.
The question compares the communication needed for one input pair with the communication needed for many pairs together.
A single universal constant would force cost to grow proportionally with the number of copies.
The protocol uses public randomness and must produce the entire answer vector correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input tuple.
Recent claimed counterexamples for relations do not resolve the chosen total-function version.

definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know \(f\) and the finite domains. A public-coin protocol selects a deterministic binary communication tree using a finite string of independent shared fair random bits, independent of the inputs. At a node, the designated player sends one bit determined by that player’s own input, the public string and the transcript so far. At termination Bob outputs a bit determined by his input, the public string and transcript. The worst-case cost is the maximum number of communicated bits over all inputs and public strings. Local computation and the public random string are free; its finite length may depend on the protocol. There is no message to reveal the public seed, no advice depending on private inputs and no restriction to one-way communication. The complexity \(R_{1/3}(f)\) is the minimum cost of a protocol whose output equals \(f(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input pair. It is finite because Alice can send an encoding of her input. Protocols may depend nonuniformly on the finite function; no uniform construction from its truth table is requested. For \(f^{\otimes k}:X^k\times Y^k\to\{0,1\}^k\), Alice and Bob receive their full tuples and Bob must output \((f(x_1,y_1),\ldots,f(x_k,y_k))\). Success probability at least \(2/3\) concerns the entire vector simultaneously on every tuple pair. The inputs need not be independent draws from a distribution: the cost and error guarantees are worst-case. The protocol may communicate across coordinates in any way. The constant \(c\) must work for all domains, functions and copy counts; a different constant for each fixed function is insufficient. Zero-communication functions impose the vacuous lower bound zero.
answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the universal constant-factor inequality, or a Lean proof of its negation: for every positive proposed constant there are a total Boolean function and copy count violating it. Refuting a version for relations, partial functions, distributional inputs or per-coordinate error alone does not refute this selected assertion. Expected communication is not the cost used here.
